title: Thermodynamics & Transport in Bioengineering
description: Conservation laws, thermodynamic driving forces, fluid mechanics, heat and mass transfer, and scaling applied to cells, tissues, and bioprocess equipment.

modifications: Expanded week 1 with control-volume selection, species and total-mass balances, transient and steady-state distinctions, residence time, reaction terms, and a signed open-system energy balance. Mapped both objectives and the practice assessment to outcome 1. Added a steady-flow energy-balance calculation so the mass-and-energy outcome has direct evidence; existing concentration and accumulation question prompts and keys remain unchanged. Added MIT OpenCourseWare Unified Engineering control-volume notes as a link-only reference.

Expanded week 3 with Fickian flux direction and units, transient diffusion, boundary conditions, diffusion and reaction time scales, the Damköhler comparison, reaction-diffusion length, and geometry and kinetic limits. Mapped both objectives to outcomes 2 and 4. Reassociated the preserved diffusion-time check with the time-scale objective and added direct flux-direction and diffusion-versus-reaction checks. Added MIT OpenCourseWare 10.37 Lecture 20 as a link-only technical reference.

Expanded week 9 with Reynolds scaling, characteristic-length conventions, the fully developed Poiseuille relation, radius sensitivity, resistance networks, entrance effects, and limits for microvascular suspensions. Mapped both objectives to outcomes 3 and 4. Added a Reynolds-number interpretation item so the stated limits are practiced directly; existing numeric prompts and keys remain unchanged. Added MIT OpenCourseWare microfluidics and fluid-mechanics resources as link-only references.

Expanded week 12 with conduction, convection and radiation rate laws; steady thermal-resistance networks; transient energy storage; lumped-capacitance assumptions; Biot and Fourier numbers; and model limits. Mapped the heat-transfer-mode objective to outcome 4 and the resistance-network objective to outcomes 1 and 4. Corrected the preserved slab-resistance item association and added direct practice comparing transfer modes; existing numeric prompts and keys remain unchanged. MIT OpenCourseWare 2.51 readings are a link-only reference.

Added an original chemical-potential and reaction-equilibrium lesson to week 1, connecting ideal-mixture activities, reaction Gibbs energy, K and an A⇌B equilibrium composition. Added nine formative items and four retrieval cards. MIT OCW 20.110J Fall 2005 calendar and Lecture 9 are link-only scope and technical references; no source text, figure or assessment was imported. The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added an original closed-system first-law and ideal-gas reading with formative practice to week 1. MIT OCW 20.110J Fall 2005 and Open Yale Courses PHYS 200 are link-only scope comparators recorded in a new scope crosswalk; no source text, figure or problem is imported.

prerequisites.statement: Differential Equations; Physics: Mechanics; General Chemistry II

outcomes.description: Write control-volume balances for mass and energy.
Apply diffusion and advection models with boundary conditions.
Estimate flow regime and pressure drop.
Use dimensional analysis to select dominant mechanisms.
Write entropy balances for closed and steady-flow systems and assess consistency with the second law.
Relate chemical-potential differences to reaction Gibbs energy and equilibrium, and calculate composition for a stated ideal mixture.
Analyze phase partitioning, nonideal mixture stability and electrochemical or osmotic driving forces under explicit thermodynamic and transport assumptions.

lesson_objectives.description: Write accumulation = in − out + generation − consumption.
Choose a control volume and distinguish steady from transient state.
Use Fick's law to determine flux direction and scale.
Compare diffusion and reaction timescales.
Compute Reynolds number and state its limits.
Apply pressure-flow relations for idealized laminar conduits.
Compare conduction, convection, and radiation.
Use a resistance network for heat or mass transfer.
Compute the oxygen profile minimum and the critical thickness for a slab or sphere with zero-order consumption.
Use a dimensionless ratio of consumption to diffusion to decide which process limits oxygen delivery.
Evaluate design levers against the assumptions of the model.
Write steady control-volume balances for mass and energy across a heated flow line and compute the heating power required.
Calculate mean velocity and Reynolds number to determine the flow regime in a tube.
Estimate pressure drop and wall shear stress for laminar flow with the Hagen–Poiseuille relation, and evaluate how they scale with diameter.
Estimate diffusion times with L²/D and compare them with consumption times and experiment durations.
Use the error-function solution to compute the concentration at a depth and time, and the time to reach a given fraction of the surface value.
Evaluate when the semi-infinite and constant-surface-concentration assumptions hold.
Compute the Péclet number from the advection and diffusion time scales and say which process controls transport.
Compute a mass-transfer coefficient for laminar tube flow and the concentration difference needed to supply a wall flux.
Evaluate what raising the flow rate does, and does not do, for delivery to a surface.
Compute the central oxygen concentration and the critical radius of a sphere with zero-order consumption.
Describe the anoxic core of a larger sphere, its radius and its share of the volume, and the thickness of the living rim.
Estimate the time a growing spheroid takes to reach its critical size and evaluate the limits of the model.
Compute the uptake rate, and the fraction of the maximum rate, at a given oxygen concentration.
Judge where the zero-order approximation is accurate and by how much it overestimates consumption elsewhere.
Evaluate how saturable uptake changes the interpretation of a critical thickness.
Compute the time constant of a body cooling or warming by convection and the time to reach a target temperature.
Compute the Biot number and decide whether the lumped assumption holds.
Compare external and internal thermal time scales and evaluate when a gradient inside the body controls the time course.
Compute the mean residence time and the wash-in and washout times of a well-mixed chamber.
Include first-order consumption and compute the steady concentration and the effective time constant.
Compare a single well-mixed volume with tanks in series and evaluate the assumption of perfect mixing.
Summarize replicate oxygen profiles by slab thickness at chosen depths.
Estimate the consumption rate from the curvature of a profile and the critical thickness from it.
Interpret a profile that reaches zero oxygen, including the thickness of the anoxic zone, and state the limits of the model.
Compute the radial oxygen drop from a channel to the edge of the tissue it supplies, and the axial drop along the channel.
Locate the lowest oxygen concentration and compare design changes (flow, channel spacing) by their effects on it.
State what each step of the model assumes and design a measurement that could show it to be wrong.
Separate entropy transfer with heat and mass from entropy generation within the modeled system.
Write closed-system and steady-flow entropy balances with consistent signs, stream terms and absolute temperatures.
Check whether a stated process is compatible with nonnegative entropy generation and distinguish entropy from energy accounting.
Calculate a reaction quotient and reaction Gibbs energy from stated activities.
Relate standard reaction Gibbs energy to an equilibrium constant and solve a one-reaction equilibrium composition.
Distinguish equilibrium conditions from reaction rates and identify assumptions in an ideal-mixture calculation.
Write and simplify the steady-flow first law for a liquid and calculate the heating power for a flowing stream.
Apply Bernoulli's equation to hydrostatic feed pressure, efflux speed and a constriction, and state when it is valid.
Use the mechanical energy balance with a Poiseuille friction loss to calculate pump work and power, and judge which terms are negligible.
Combine phase partitioning with a conserved solute balance.
Distinguish a lever balance from determining coexistence.
Use free-energy curvature to diagnose local mixture stability.
Keep activity corrections and concentration ratios consistent.
Combine chemical and electrical contributions with a declared direction.
Evaluate a coupled energy ledger without claiming a mechanism.
Distinguish an ion equilibrium voltage from an arbitrary multi-ion membrane voltage.
Connect osmotic pressure to a direction-labeled solvent flux law.
Derive explicit positivity bounds from the actual balance stencil.
Verify a conservative update and its unit of stored amount.
Use a continuum reference to verify cell-centered boundary assembly.
Distinguish positivity, conservation, accuracy and model validity.
Build an activity-consistent partition and conservation report.
Report conditional phase amounts without conflating local stability and coexistence.
Verify an electrochemical coupling budget with its next-integer failure.
Combine osmotic flux with evolving closed-reservoir balances.
Verify local face transfers against a global discrete amount balance.
Separate reaction-diffusion resolution and global conservation checks.
Apply ΔU = Q − W to a closed system with the course's sign convention, and distinguish state functions from path functions.
Compute the work, heat and temperature change of isothermal, isobaric, isochoric and reversible adiabatic processes of an ideal gas from C_v, C_p and γ.
Compare reversible and irreversible expansions between the same states, and connect the difference to entropy generation.

duration.equivalent_structure: Proposed 14-week undergraduate scope only. Week 1 now links control-volume, closed-system first-law and ideal-gas, entropy-balance, and chemical-potential/reaction-equilibrium readings in one thermodynamic foundation; the four former compact prototype readings in weeks 1, 3, 9 and 12 also have expanded instruction alongside original lessons on residence time, transient diffusion, oxygen limits in slabs and spheroids, saturable uptake, tubing and pressure drop, advection and diffusion together, and lumped heat transfer. Week 10 pairs the tubing balances with steady-flow energy balances, Bernoulli and friction losses. Week 8 is a synthetic-data lab on oxygen depth profiles and week 14 is a lesson on a perfused construct with a hypoxic center that prepares the course case. Weeks 13–14 add an optional heat-generation slab project with rehearsal practice and milestone self-checks. All activities are open, ungraded practice. There are no graded homework sets, exams or graded project, and workload has not been measured, so this schedule is not evidence of semester equivalence.

weeks.title: Thermodynamic foundations: control volumes, the closed-system first law, entropy and chemical equilibrium

Transient diffusion: penetration depth, the error function and equilibration times

Oxygen in a spheroid: the critical radius, the anoxic core and the living rim
When zero order fails: Michaelis–Menten uptake and a softer edge to the limit
Virtual lab: oxygen depth profiles in cell-laden slabs
Perfusing a culture through tubing: control-volume balances, pressure drop and energy balances
Advection and diffusion together: the Péclet number and mass-transfer coefficients
Heat transfer: lumped capacitance, the Biot number and thermal time scales; optional heat-generation slab project

lessons.title: Control volumes and conservation
lessons.worked_example: A rigid 100 L well-mixed tank receives and discharges 2 L/min, has inlet concentration 5 g/L, and consumes the species at k=0.02 min⁻¹. Its balance is V dC/dt=Q(Cin−C)−kVC; the steady concentration is 2.5 g/L. The liquid volume is constant, but species concentration is transient until it reaches that balance.

lessons.title: Diffusion, reaction, and characteristic length
lessons.worked_example: For D=2×10⁻⁹ m²/s, L=200 μm and first-order k=0.05 s⁻¹, tD≈L²/D=20 s and tR≈1/k=20 s, so Da≈1. The reaction-diffusion length √(D/k)=200 μm matches the modeled distance. Diffusion and reaction are comparable here; this scale check does not replace a geometry-specific profile.

lessons.title: Fluid mechanics and microvascular flow
lessons.worked_example: For water-like fluid with ρ=1000 kg/m³, mean U=1 mm/s, specified L=100 μm, and μ=10⁻³ Pa·s, Re=0.1. In a separate rigid tube with R=0.50 mm, ℓ=0.10 m, μ=10⁻³ Pa·s and ΔP=100 Pa, Poiseuille flow gives Q≈2.45×10⁻⁸ m³/s. Halving the radius at the same pressure drop reduces the ideal Q sixteenfold; neither calculation validates the idealization for a compliant, branching microvascular bed.

lessons.title: Heat transfer and coupled transport
lessons.worked_example: For a 0.020 m slab with k=0.50 W/(m·K) and A=0.10 m², Rcond=L/(kA)=0.40 K/W. With h=100 W/(m²·K) over the same area, Rconv=1/(hA)=0.10 K/W. At steady state the series resistance is 0.50 K/W, so a 50 K driving difference gives 100 W; the slab and fluid-film drops are 40 K and 10 K.

lessons.title: Oxygen limits in thick constructs: zero-order uptake, critical thickness and time scales
lessons.worked_example: With D = 2×10⁻⁹ m²/s, C₀ = 0.2 mol/m³ and q = 0.02 mol/(m³·s), L_c = 200 µm; a 150 µm slab has C_min = 0.0875 mol/m³, doubling C₀ gives 283 µm, and a 100 µm slab has φ² = 0.50.

modules.title: Perfusion tubing: balances and pressure drop

lessons.title: Perfusing a culture through tubing: control-volume balances, Reynolds number and pressure drop
lessons.worked_example: At 2.0 mL/min in a 1.0 mm tube, Re = 54.4 (laminar), ΔP over 0.5 m is 529.7 Pa (sixteen times more at half the diameter), wall shear is 0.2648 Pa, and heating from 22 to 37 °C takes 2.09 W.

modules.title: Energy balances on flowing systems: the steady-flow first law, Bernoulli and friction losses

lessons.title: Energy balances on flowing systems: the steady-flow first law, Bernoulli and friction losses
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic circuit carries medium at 20 mL/min through 1.5 m of 2.0 mm tubing (Re ≈ 212) with a 0.50 m lift. Warming it from 20 °C to 37 °C needs 23.7 W; the Poiseuille loss is 1.27 kPa, the total 6.18 kPa needs 2.06 mW of hydraulic power and 8.24 mW of pump input at 25% efficiency, about three thousand times less than the heater.

lessons.title: Transient diffusion: penetration depth, the error function and equilibration times
lessons.worked_example: For a synthetic solute with D = 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s at a constant surface concentration of 1.0 mol/m³, the concentration at 300 μm after 120 s is 0.540 mol/m³ and the half-time at that depth is 99 s; with D = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s, diffusion across 1 mm takes about 500 s and the half-time at 500 μm is 137 s.

lessons.title: Advection and diffusion together: the Péclet number and mass-transfer coefficients
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic tube of 0.5 mm diameter with U = 1.0 mm/s and D = 3.0 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s has a Péclet number of 167 over 0.5 mm, k_c = 21.96 μm/s and needs a concentration difference of 0.0091 mol/m³ to supply 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol/(m²·s); the lesson's 1 mm channel at 0.2 mm/s has Pe = 100, k_c = 7.32 μm/s and needs 0.0152 mol/m³ for a confluent monolayer.

lessons.title: Oxygen in a spheroid: the critical radius, the anoxic core and why the rim is not a constant thickness
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic spheroid with D = 1.5 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s, C₀ = 0.15 mol/m³ and q = 0.03 mol/(m³·s) has a critical radius of 212.1 μm and keeps 0.042 mol/m³ at its centre at 180 μm, reaching the critical size from 80 μm in 127 h at a 30 h doubling time; the lesson's sphere has R_c = 346.4 μm, a 130.5 μm core (3.5% of the volume) at 400 μm and a 243.3 μm rim at 500 μm.

lessons.title: When zero order fails: Michaelis–Menten oxygen uptake and a softer edge to the limit
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic cell with V_max 0.03 mol/(m³·s) and K_m 0.01 mol/m³ takes up oxygen at 75% of V_max at 0.03 mol/m³ (a zero-order model overestimates it by 1.33), needs 0.19 mol/m³ for 95% of V_max and is first order with rate constant 3.0 per second at low oxygen; in the lesson's slab the Michaelis–Menten minimum at 200 μm is 0.0229 mol/m³ where the zero-order model gives zero.

lessons.title: Heat transfer: lumped capacitance, the Biot number and thermal time scales
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic water-like sphere of 6 mm diameter with h = 25 W/(m²·K) has τ = 167 s and Bi = 0.042, and warms from 22 to 35 °C in 337 s toward 37 °C; the 10 mm sphere in the lesson has τ = 697 s in air and 19.8 min to cool from 37 to 10 °C, but Bi = 1.39 in a bath, where the lumped model fails.

lessons.title: Well-mixed chambers: residence time, wash-in and washout, and tanks in series
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic 5 mL chamber fed at 2 mL/min has a residence time of 2.5 min, washes out to 1% in 11.5 min, reaches 0.667 of the feed concentration with first-order uptake k = 0.2 per minute (effective time constant 1.67 min), and two equal tanks in series reach 0.594 at t = τ; the lesson's 10 mL chamber at 0.5 mL/min has τ = 20 min and reaches 95% after 59.9 min.

lessons.title: Virtual lab 1: oxygen depth profiles in cell-laden slabs
lessons.worked_example: The synthetic slabs give a consumption rate of 0.02 mol/(m³·s) from the 100 μm profile and a critical thickness of 200 μm; the 300 μm slab reaches zero oxygen at 200 μm, leaving an anoxic zone of 100 μm, and the 200 μm and 300 μm profiles coincide down to the critical depth.

modules.title: A perfused construct with a hypoxic center

lessons.title: A perfused construct with a hypoxic center: advection supplies the channel, diffusion supplies the tissue
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic channel of 75 μm radius feeding tissue to 150 μm at 4 μL/min has a radial drop of 0.0268 mol/m³ and an axial drop of 0.0954 mol/m³, so the lowest concentration at the outlet end is 0.0777 mol/m³; the lesson's channel loses 0.113 mol/m³ along its length and 0.064 mol/m³ radially, leaving 0.023 mol/m³ at the outlet end, and needs 13.1 μL/min or channels at 150 μm to stay above 0.05 mol/m³.

lessons.title: Entropy balances and irreversibility
lessons.worked_example: For an adiabatic steady-flow device with one inlet and outlet at 0.10 kg/s and specific entropies 2.0 and 2.3 kJ/(kg·K), the stream balance requires entropy generation of 0.10(2.3−2.0)=0.03 kW/K. The positive value satisfies the second law for the stipulated example; no real device or fluid is represented.

lessons.title: Chemical potential and reaction equilibrium
lessons.worked_example: At 298 K, K=4 for ideal A⇌B gives ΔrG°=−3.43 kJ/mol. At activities aA=1 and aB=0.20, ΔrG=−7.43 kJ/mol; a closed 1.20 mM batch reaches [A]=0.24 mM and [B]=0.96 mM at equilibrium.

lessons.title: Slab project guide: steady heat generation, an energy check and the lumped limit (optional, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: For a synthetic slab with L = 0.005 m, k = 0.25 W/(m·K), q‴ = 30,000 W/m³, h = 50 W/(m²·K) and T∞ = 30 °C, the surface is 33.0 °C and the center 34.5 °C, the face flux 150 W/m² matches convection, and Bi = 1.0: a lumped 33.0 °C estimate misses the center by 1.5 °C, half the rise above the fluid.

modules.title: Activities, phase partitioning and nonideal stability

lessons.title: Activities, phase partitioning and nonideal stability
lessons.worked_example: Use n=cα(Vα+Kp Vβ), so cα=0.010/0.005=2 mol/m³ and cβ=6 mol/m³. Their amounts are 0.004 and 0.006 mol, summing to the supplied total; the ratio is three. Concentrations differ at equilibrium because the phase standard-state contributions can differ.

modules.title: Electrochemical potentials, coupled energy and solvent flux

lessons.title: Electrochemical potentials, coupled energy and solvent flux
lessons.worked_example: The chemical term is RT ln2≈1728.8477 J/mol and the electrical term is −964.85 J/mol. Their sum is approximately 763.99770 J/mol, so this declared transfer is uphill. Reversing the transfer reverses both terms; changing the ion charge reverses only its electrical contribution.

modules.title: Finite-volume diffusion, boundary geometry and conservation

lessons.title: Finite-volume diffusion, boundary geometry and conservation
lessons.worked_example: For no sink, r≤0.5 gives Δt≤0.5Δx²/D=2.5 s. Adding the first-order sink changes the self coefficient, giving Δt≤1/(2D/Δx²+k)=2 s. These are sufficient positivity tests for this no-flux uniform formulation, not universal boundary or accuracy guarantees.

lessons.title: Assignment 1: phase and free-energy ledger
lessons.worked_example: The concentration ratio is 4×0.8/1.6=2. The balance denominator is 0.004+2×0.001=0.006 m³, giving cα=2 and cβ=4 mol/m³. Amounts 0.008 and 0.004 mol close the supplied total; the corrected activity ratio is four.

modules.title: Assignment 2: coupled reservoirs and energy ledgers

lessons.title: Assignment 2: coupled reservoirs and energy ledgers
lessons.worked_example: Add RT ln3 to −964.85 J/mol for the transfer cost, then check integer multiples against 10000 J per event. Five transfers are favorable while six exceed the supply. The ledger does not demonstrate a physical coupling mechanism.

lessons.title: Assignment 3: conservative transport verification
lessons.worked_example: Use the old vector in every component: the update is [0.2,0.6,0.2,0]. Its sum remains one. A mixed-time in-place update implements a different algorithm, so both the first-step vector and global total belong in the tests.

modules.title: The closed-system first law: work, heat and ideal-gas processes

lessons.title: The closed-system first law: work, heat and ideal-gas processes
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic sealed syringe holds 0.0200 mol of a diatomic ideal gas at 300 K and 100 kPa (V₁ = 0.4988 L). Compressed reversibly to half its volume, the gas reaches 395.9 K and 263.9 kPa with 39.85 J of work done on it when the compression is adiabatic, and stays at 300 K and 200 kPa with 34.58 J of work done on it, all of it leaving as heat, when the compression is isothermal.

grading_policy.attempt_policy: Unlimited formative retries; no summative grade is awarded.
grading_policy.solution_release: Public practice solutions may be shown after an attempt. They are not production exam keys.
grading_policy.late_policy: No deadlines or late penalties exist in this partial package.

accessibility.diagram_policy: The seed package contains no imported diagrams; newly authored diagrams require descriptions and individual license tracking.
known_issues: Unicode equations require structured mathematical alternatives and assistive-technology review.

history.summary: Preserved original compact prototype content in separate manifests and readings; labeled partial without semester or credit equivalency.

The package remains partial and unreviewed.

The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added a proposed 14-week schedule; seven original lessons (residence time, wash-in and washout; transient diffusion and the error function; advection, diffusion and the Péclet number; oxygen in a spheroid with an anoxic core; Michaelis–Menten uptake and the limits of zero order; lumped heat transfer and the Biot number; and a perfused construct with a hypoxic center, which prepares the course case); and a synthetic-data lab on oxygen depth profiles in slabs. Compared the course with a second university comparator, Open Yale Courses PHYS 200 Lectures 20–24, alongside MIT OCW 20.110J Fall 2005, in a new scope crosswalk that records covered, shallow, absent and local-extension topics. No local reading, practice item or card used the terms state function, internal energy, ideal gas, Carnot or heat engine, although both comparators teach the closed-system foundation (MIT Lectures 1–4; Yale Lectures 21–23). A new week-1 reading defines state and path functions, applies ΔU = Q − W with the course's sign convention, develops the ideal gas with C_v, C_p and γ, works the isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric and isochoric processes of one gas, and compares a reversible with an irreversible expansion, connecting the lost work to the entropy generated. Added three objectives, 13 practice items and four retrieval cards, and corrected the stated range of items per original lesson. Heat engines and the Carnot cycle (Yale only), thermochemistry and the Joule–Thomson experiment (MIT only), statistical thermodynamics, single-component phase equilibria, solvation and the Debye length remain recorded gaps. The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

The heat-generation slab project is optional and ungraded. Its five milestones are Case studio self-checks whose private drafts are never submitted or scored; the rehearsal practice uses a separate synthetic slab, and no software check evaluates a learner's derivation or written interpretation. Milestone weeks are planning suggestions, not measured workload or deadlines.

New thermodynamics and finite-volume readings develop selected phase/activity, electrochemical/osmotic/coupled-energy and conservative discretization models with three open coursework packets. General nonideal phase diagrams, statistical thermodynamics, self-consistent multi-ion fields and general CFD remain outside the selected combined scope. Code, derivations, plots and reports are not automatically evaluated; workload and qualified review remain open.
